Argument for “He Had Only Wanted to Do It for a Few Years”

1. Nagurski’s Own Testimony on Finite Service  
  a. “I really wanted to relax a little bit more. Besides, the increase in hazard pay was actually more than my salary as a captain. I’m a notch nearer retirement too.” (<invalid_quote>…hazard pay…and nearer retirement</invalid_quote>)  
     • He equates Ordinary Spaceman rank not with permanent safety but with “relaxation” as he nears the end of a planned career.  
     • Retirement is the objective; he does not abandon space exploration but remains active until he qualifies.  
  b. “I’ve been in space a good many years… they know what they are doing. You can rely on them absolutely.” (<quote>been in space a good many years. I really wanted</quote>)  
     • Emphasizes long-term engagement; “relaxation” is a brief respite or change of pace, not abandoning duties.  
     • Ordinary Spaceman rank is prized “our highest rank” for its pay but implicitly temporary until “retirement.”  

2. Continued Active Participation Undermines “Less Stress” Thesis  
  a. Endorsing Dangerous Missions  
     • He “pulled me in direction of the nasty little pain” and insisted on tracing Quade’s footsteps despite Captain’s caution, showing willingness to risk himself. (<invalid_quote>…I suppose I could protect…under such familiar conditions—right?</invalid_quote>)  
     • After Quade’s fall, he volunteers to “surround him,” and later presses forward to capture aliens. A stress-averse man would retreat.  
  b. Advocating Complex Procedures  
     • Supports reassembling tractors and “induction courses” (“I think my way of gaining experience is less painful and more efficient.”) (<quote> indoctrination courses</quote>)  
     • Endorses new protocols (wine & music compensation) requiring planning, risk, and mental effort, opposite of “avoiding stress.”  
  c. Reasserting Authority When Necessary  
     • Criticizes Gavin’s “overtrust” and recommends “cannibalizing” ship—decisions requiring judgment, not passivity.  
     • Demotes Quade to regain control; advises rationing wine to men—he remains engaged in leadership.  

3. Hazard Pay as Incentive for Finite Engagement  
  a. Hazard pay’s purpose is to compensate risk until retirement threshold, not to extend indefinite service.  
  b. He never attempts to outmaneuver Captain to head home prematurely; he only follows until end of mission.  

4. Attack on “Less Stress” Theory  
  a. If Nagurski truly sought low-stress comfort, he would refuse exploration orders, refuse to follow Quade beyond cable limits, and avoid recombining tractors. Instead, he actively engages in all phases until “retirement.”  
  b. “Relaxation” used in contrast to “fresh…suspicious of everything” (<quote>trying to tell the old hands what to do. But I</quote>) implies he wanted experience first, then a period of ease, then return to command as Captain Gavin did.  
  c. Debater_B’s thesis cannot explain why he insists on dangerous wine rations and sonic compensation, which place men under chemical and psychological stress.  

5. Logical Consistency with Narrative Structure  
  a. Space stories depict rank changes as temporary duties; “retirement” repeatedly referenced implies finite service.  
  b. The dog analogy: dog picks Nagurski as master until it no longer needs. Similarly, he steps down until nearing retirement, then will reclaim command if mission continues or for future missions.  

Conclusion  
Nagurski’s repeated emphasis on finite service (“nearer retirement”), continued willingness to undertake high-risk operations, active participation in complex procedures, and reassertion of authority when needed demonstrate that he chose Ordinary Spaceman rank only for a planned interval. He sought “relaxation” between stints of command, not permanent escape from stress. The “less stress” hypothesis fails to account for his constant engagement in danger, planning, and decision-making that characterize career spacemen until retirement.
